solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sap scattered with spore, one in strange attachment for parasite

indicators.note: things scattered are thrown about out of order, so the letters of sap and spore get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: one item placed in another means the single letter sits inside the word for strange

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A botanist describes the sticky sap and scattered spores of some odd parasitic growth.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled sap and spore come first, then I goes inside RUM to finish APPRESSORIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: An appressorium is the flattened pad a parasitic fungus grows to cling to its host before penetrating it.

clue.text: One against exemplar of industry digs art possibly, fan of modernism?

parts.note: a means one, as in a single item

indicators.note: possibly signals that the preceding words could be arranged another way

parts.note: v. is the abbreviation for versus, against
the ant is the proverbial model of hard work
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone opposed to a hard-working figure excavates artworks, perhaps as a lover of the new.
explanation.walkthrough: The ant as an emblem of industry comes from Proverbs: 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard'.
explanation.definitionFit: An avant-gardist champions experimental, innovative art, the kind of person who embraces modernist movements.

clue.text: Getting up, make space for former idol

indicators.note: in a down entry, getting up means the letters climb from the bottom, read in reverse order

parts.note: to do is to make, as in do a drawing
a gap is a space

explanation.surface: An instruction to clear room, on rising, for a fallen idol.
explanation.walkthrough: DO and GAP are joined, then read upwards to give PAGOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Pagod is an archaic word for a pagoda and also for the idol housed in one, hence a former term for an idol.

clue.text: A commonplace person

parts.note: surface reading: an ordinary, unremarkable individual
setter's reading: this is the competition word, given by definition alone; commonplace here means dull and unimaginative

explanation.walkthrough: This is the Azed clue-writing competition entry, so only a definition is printed and solvers find the word from crossings.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides a writer of prose, Chambers gives a prosaist as a matter-of-fact, unpoetic person, someone dull and ordinary.

clue.text: Take on gardener's enemy, something found in plant cells

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions
aphis is the greenfly, a garden pest

explanation.surface: Advice to tackle the gardener's foe, something lurking inside the cells of plants.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts R above APHIS. 'Take on' reads as a phrase meaning to confront, but take alone is R.
explanation.definitionFit: A raphis (plural raphides) is a needle-shaped crystal of calcium oxalate occurring inside plant cells.

clue.text: What streaker at Lord's may do in interval?

definitions.text: What streaker at Lord's may do
definitions.meaning: a naked runner on a cricket pitch would halt the current set of six balls

explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground; an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end, so a streaker could stop the over.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopover is a short break in a journey, a pause or interval between legs of travel.

clue.text: Military caps raised, king ignored aid to road-holding

indicators.note: in a down entry, something raised is read upwards, from bottom to top
what is ignored is left out, so the royal letter is dropped

parts.note: kepis are French military caps with flat tops
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Soldiers' hats are lifted while the monarch is snubbed, all somehow about a car's grip.
explanation.walkthrough: KEPIS read upwards is SIPEK; dropping the K leaves SIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sipe is a thin slit cut in a tyre tread to improve grip on wet roads.

clue.text: Smoke rising round centre of verdure creeps over the border

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from bottom to top
going round something means wrapping about it, enclosing the other piece

parts.note: segar is an old variant spelling of cigar

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, here of a seven-letter word

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters

explanation.surface: Smoke drifts up around the greenery while creeping figures slip across a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: SEGAR read upwards is RAGES, and D goes inside it. 'Over the border' means in Scotland, where a radge is a wild or crazy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Radge is Scots slang for an unpleasant or unhinged person, which matches creeps used as a noun for nasty people.

clue.text: Trees a Filipino reared, millions planted

indicators.note: in a down entry, something reared up stands on end, its letters read upwards
something planted is set into the ground, so this letter is set inside the other

parts.note: the Sulu are a people of the southern Philippines
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A Filipino grew trees, millions of them, planted out.
explanation.walkthrough: SULU read upwards is ULUS, and M goes into the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulmus is the botanical genus name of the elms, so it stands for a group of trees.

clue.text: Burgher poet, German, sister translated

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so the letters are converted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A German townsman-poet's sister had his work translated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German' looks like part of the definition, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mastersingers were medieval German guild poets drawn from the craftsmen and burghers of towns like Nuremberg.

clue.text: Lizard, large or small variety and tailless

indicators.note: without a tail means the final letter is cut off the word

parts.note: var. is the botanical abbreviation for variety
taken as written, before losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A lizard of any size or kind, missing its tail as lizards sometimes are.
explanation.walkthrough: Lizards really do shed their tails, which hides that 'tailless' acts on the word and.
explanation.definitionFit: A varan is a monitor lizard, a family whose members range from small species to the huge Komodo dragon.

clue.text: Part of botanical label for marsh plant

indicators.note: part of means only a stretch of the following words is wanted

parts.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A fragment of a botanical tag identifies a plant from the marshes.
explanation.definitionFit: Calla is the bog arum, Calla palustris, a plant of wet marshy ground.

clue.text: Seats may get attention from me!

definitions.text: Seats may get attention from me!

parts.note: surface reading: chairs whose seats need reweaving
setter's reading: seats are backsides too, and a punisher with a rod gives them attention

explanation.walkthrough: Seats works both as chair seats, woven from cane, and as bottoms, which a schoolmaster's cane once found.
explanation.definitionFit: A caner is either someone who weaves cane chair seats or someone who beats with a cane.

clue.text: Father having trouble writing accompaniment for Indian?

parts.note: pop is an informal word for dad
ado is fuss or trouble
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Dad is struggling to write something to go with an Indian person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' means an Indian meal, as in 'going for an Indian', not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Poppadoms are thin crisp lentil wafers served alongside an Indian restaurant meal.

clue.text: Bit of nutmeg, hot, in soup embellished blow-out

indicators.note: something embellished is dressed up and altered, so these letters are reworked
a bit of a word here is just its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dash of nutmeg and some heat dress up a soup for a big feast.
explanation.walkthrough: Blow-out here is a hearty meal, not a burst tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosh-up is British slang for a large, lavish meal, as is a blow-out.

clue.text: Stuff our country is short of and as of old

indicators.note: being short of something means lacking it, so those letters go missing

parts.note: the setter's country, writing in a British paper
the letters removed
ut is Latin for as, an old form

explanation.surface: A complaint that the nation lacks the stuff it once had.
explanation.walkthrough: ENGLAND loses AND to leave ENGL. 'and' looks like a joining word, but it is the piece to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Englut is an archaic verb meaning to gorge or cram, so to stuff, as with food.

clue.text: That's some book, I admit, retreating — I'm beaten for sure

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read right to left
some of the following words means only part of their run of letters is used

parts.note: the end of the first word, the single letter and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone backing down concedes that's quite a book and admits defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm beaten' reads as admitting defeat, but the thing that gets beaten is a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: The daiko is a Japanese drum, an instrument that is certainly struck when played.

clue.text: Cavalry piece? Nelly's holding on

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it inside, so the second word goes within the first

parts.note: a nelly is a giant petrel, a large seabird
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Nelly clings on to a weapon from the cavalry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nelly' looks like a woman's name, but a nelly is the giant petrel. The 's is 'is', joining the bird to holding.
explanation.definitionFit: A petronel was a large horse-pistol of the 16th and 17th centuries, carried by cavalry troops.

clue.text: Round start of opera strengthens tenor last of all

indicators.note: going round means surrounding, so the next piece is enclosed

parts.note: to rearm is to strengthen with fresh weapons

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: Opera talk: the opening strengthens the tenor, who comes in right at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: REARMS goes round O, then T is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearmost means furthest back, the very last in a line.

clue.text: Old fur, bits regularly shed by girlies

indicators.note: dropping bits at a regular interval means every other letter goes and the rest stay

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Young women discard their worn-out fur coats.
explanation.definitionFit: Gris is an obsolete word for a grey fur, such as squirrel, once used for trimming garments.

clue.text: Love poetry set before HM editor lost?

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
verse is poetry
ER is Elizabeth Regina, Her Majesty

explanation.surface: Love poetry put before the Queen, with its editor gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: To oversee once also meant to overlook or fail to notice, so an editor who has lost track of an error might be called an overseer.
explanation.definitionFit: An overseer supervises, as an editor does, while the archaic sense of oversee as overlook gives the 'lost' joke.

clue.text: E.g. Bunthorne, upset about these being distributed

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first piece is wrapped around the second

parts.note: ate in the sense of 'what's eating you?', meaning troubled

indicators.note: things distributed are spread around, so the letters are dealt out in a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The poet Bunthorne is upset at these being handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunthorne is the affected poet in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience, a satire on the aesthetic movement. 'Upset' looks like the anagram signal but is ATE, as in 'what's eating him'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunthorne is an example of an aesthete, someone devoted to beauty and art, and the operetta lampoons that type.

clue.text: Despot, all but the last one's seen in purple?

indicators.note: seen in means appearing inside, so the single letter is placed within
everything except the final letter is kept, so the word is trimmed at the end

parts.note: a tyrant is a despot
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A despot, nearly all of him, appears clothed in purple, as emperors were.
explanation.walkthrough: TYRANT loses its T to give TYRAN, and I goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyrian purple was the costly dye from Tyre, so Tyrian can describe that colour; the question mark flags the indirect fit.

clue.text: What'll be heard encouraging dance from the audience?

indicators.note: what reaches an audience is what they hear, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: the hay is an old country dance

explanation.surface: Shouts of encouragement for a dance come from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The hay (or hey) is an old English country dance with interweaving lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Heigh is an interjection used to cheer someone on or call attention, so it is a cry of encouragement one would hear.

clue.text: What'll come from murder motive as reported?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its sound matters

parts.note: a cause is a motive

explanation.surface: A detective wonders what motive lies behind a murder.
explanation.walkthrough: A murder is the collective noun for crows, so 'murder' points at birds, not a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Caws are the harsh calls of crows, the noise a murder of crows makes.

clue.text: Candied peel? This, aged, is misused in decorating

indicators.note: something misused is handled wrongly, so the remaining letters are put in a new order
this word, the aged one, is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: the letters removed
the longer word

explanation.surface: An old cook complains that this is wrongly used to decorate cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of AGED out of DECORATING, leaving CORTIN, and rearrange. 'This, aged,' is read as this word, aged, being misused in decorating.
explanation.definitionFit: Citron is a large citrus fruit whose thick rind is candied and used in baking, so candied peel is an example.

clue.text: Foreign gent erected guttering for Scots

indicators.note: in a down entry, something erected is stood upright, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a rone is a Scottish word for a roof gutter or downpipe

explanation.surface: A foreign gentleman put up gutters in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Señor is the Spanish title for a man, the equivalent of Mr or sir.

clue.text: Highland clamour, increasingly restrained, from the right

indicators.note: reading from the right in an across entry means going backwards

parts.note: dry can mean restrained or understated, and drier is more so

explanation.surface: A Highland racket grows steadily more muted on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Highland signals a Scottish word: reird (or rerde) is a din or uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: Reird is a Scots word for a loud noise or uproar, a clamour.

clue.text: Nothing surmounts this compact for Danish conurbation

indicators.note: the round letter sits on top of the answer to make the place, so it is the part to take away

parts.note: Odense is Denmark's third-largest city
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: Nothing beats this compact pact for a Danish urban area.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: put O on top of the answer and you get the Danish city ODENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Dense means tightly packed together, which is what compact means as an adjective.

clue.text: Source of insecticide? Show contempt about lapse

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word wraps around the second

parts.note: to dis is slang for to disrespect
to err is to lapse

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a moment's slip in the hunt for a bug killer.
explanation.definitionFit: Derris is a tropical climbing plant whose roots yield rotenone, used as an insecticide.

clue.text: Learn origin of primordial ooze

parts.note: to see is to learn or find out

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Study how life began in the primordial ooze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primordial ooze' reads as one phrase, but ooze alone is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To seep is to leak slowly through, the same as to ooze.

clue.text: Early Irish settlers fixing sign round thoroughfare briefly

indicators.note: briefly means in shortened form, so only the abbreviation is used
going round means surrounding, so the first word encloses the second

parts.note: an omen is a sign
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Early settlers in Ireland put up a sign round the main road.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ostmen were the Norse (Danish) settlers who founded towns in Ireland, named as men from the east.

clue.text: Occupying lodgings mostly, ten awfully hard-up

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: digs is British slang for rented lodgings, so occupying them is being in digs

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Ten people crammed into rented rooms, and terribly short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: Digs is British slang for rented rooms; IN DIGS loses its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigent describes someone poor and needy, lacking money, which is to say hard-up.

clue.text: Whence topees are made, coloured rings going round

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: halos are coloured rings, as around the moon

explanation.surface: Pith helmets are made from a plant, with bands of colour around them.
explanation.walkthrough: A topee (or sola topee) is a lightweight sun helmet worn in the tropics.
explanation.definitionFit: Solah, also sola, is the Indian swamp plant whose pith is used to make topees, so it is their material.

clue.text: Some useless officers retreating in trench

indicators.note: retreating means moving backwards, so the letters read right to left
some means only part of the following words is wanted

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Hopeless officers pulling back into a trench, a wartime scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A fosse is a ditch or moat, especially one dug in fortifications, so a trench.

clue.text: I may redesign plot — reset linen rat-traps I abandoned

indicators.note: reset means set out again in a different arrangement, so the letters are reordered
what is abandoned is left behind, so this letter is taken out

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
the letter removed

explanation.surface: A gardener plans to redo the plot, resetting rat-traps and laying aside linen.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks as the answer: a transplanter moves plants about, redesigning a garden plot.
explanation.definitionFit: A transplanter is a person or tool that moves plants from one place to another, reshaping a bed.
